Q: Linux shell script to know if the directory (or file) has 777 permission A:

Use:

find /Temp -maxdepth  0  -perm 777

This will output /Temp if the permission is 777.

Note that you can put ! in front of -perm, and the it will output if mismatch.

Q: What does Kubernetes actually do? A:

If your app needs an entire server to itself, you probably wouldn’t use kubernetes.

If you have a few different apps, and you want to run them on a fleet of machines (with each host running several different workloads at once), and you want to handle fluctuating pulses in workload (traffic) by dynamically scaling the number of copies of each app independently, then you have the use-case to appreciate kubernetes.

Kubernetes is an open source way to facilitate automatically scaling the number of copies of each app, allocating copies to particular hosts (accounting for resource requirements and available capacity), dynamically routing outside traffic to these app instances, testing for nonresponsive copies and routing traffic around them (and resetting them if they stay nonresponsive), connecting network storage volumes to specific hosts where an app needs it, dynamically maintaining internal DNS (and container IPs) to simplify communication between microservices, securely distributing credentials between containers (helping limit the scope so that it is difficult for one compromised app to escalate and impact others), and providing standardised tools and configuration to administer all of this.

Kubernetes is oriented towards avoiding outages of production services, by using redundancy to facilitate rolling maintenance and failure tolerance, and scaling to accomodate traffic surges.

Kubernetes is composed of many interchangeable components with narrow functions (similar to the UNIX philosophy). Perhaps the central component is a representation of the current and target state of the cluster, held in a distributed database and manipulated (by other components) through an API microservice. This may be hosted on master nodes, along with components for allocating containers among worker node hosts, and components for various other control loops that monitor the cluster and perturb it towards the target state. There is a CLI tool for inputting the target state from configuration manifests. There is software that runs on each worker node (including the runtime for containers, drivers for cluster networking and network storage, and a client service for coordinating with the master nodes). There is also an ecosystem of related software, such as tools for packaging complex app deployments, or for improving observability of all workloads running on the cluster.

Some cloud vendors may also offer proprietary equivalents to Kubernetes, for example AWS ECS performs a similar role. Note that Kubernetes is for containerised services, and that for RESTful web services each container image must include its own web server to listen for and handle request traffic. This contrasts with platforms that handle the network connections and translate directly to function invocations, such as inetd, CGI or AWS Lambda.

Q: How do I measure time in C? A:

I would use the QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency functions of the Windows API.

Call the former before and after the block and subtract (current − old) to get the number of "ticks" between the instances. Divide this by the value obtained by the latter function to get the duration in seconds.

Q: OCR output contains “garbage” characters after special symbols (mojibake / control chars) — how to reliably clean before returning from LLM? A:

I'd be inclined to think that:

  1. somewhere in the pipeline there is a step incorrectly encoding or decoding the text, that would explain some of the errors,

  2. From the description the OCR stage, I guess OCR uses an LLM in some way, if so, the LLM is the likely source of the control and formatting characters. They wouldn't occur in traditional OCR.
